# Photometric and Image Reconstruction Losses

Also called: Composite Image Loss, Photometric Regularization

## Overview
This family defines the objective functions used to align rendered radiance field images with ground-truth observations while enforcing physical plausibility through regularization. It solves the ill-posed nature of inverse volume rendering by combining pixel-wise fidelity metrics with constraints on geometry, motion, and density. It differs from simple photometric loss by explicitly incorporating visibility weighting, multi-resolution consistency, and structural regularization to suppress artifacts in occluded regions, empty space, and dynamic elements.

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves minimizing a weighted sum of a photometric reconstruction term and one or more regularization terms. The photometric term measures the discrepancy between the rendered color $\mathbf{C}_{\text{rendered}}$ and the ground-truth color $\mathbf{C}_{\text{gt}}$. Common metrics include L1 loss, L2 loss, and Structural Similarity (SSIM). Regularization terms enforce properties such as spatial smoothness (Total Variation), static background priors, or geometric constraints (e.g., Gaussian scaling limits). The total loss $\mathcal{L}$ is generally structured as:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{photo}} + \sum_i w_i \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}, i} $$
where $w_i$ are hyperparameters balancing the components.

## Subtopics

### [Composite Image Loss with Visibility Weighting](4262-composite-image-loss-with-visibility-weighting.md)
This method aligns rendered images with references while suppressing errors in occluded or unobserved regions [4262-composite-image-loss-with-visibility-weighting]. It sets itself apart by masking the L1 and SSIM terms with a visibility map $V_M$, ensuring supervision is only applied to visible pixels, while retaining a full-image perceptual loss (LPIPS) [4262-composite-image-loss-with-visibility-weighting]. Choose this when dealing with scenes containing significant occlusion or when a visibility mask is available.

### [Composite Photometric and Regularization Loss](9355-composite-photometric-and-regularization-loss.md)
This method optimizes radiance field models from monocular video by combining photometric fidelity with regularization for physical plausibility [9355-composite-photometric-and-regularization-loss]. It differs by explicitly penalizing artifacts like thin Gaussians, non-static background noise, and discontinuous motion fields, which are critical for stable convergence in dynamic scenes [9355-composite-photometric-and-regularization-loss]. Choose this for dynamic scene reconstruction or when using voxel/Gaussian representations requiring strong geometric priors.

### Composite RGB and Entropy Loss
This variant combines RGB reconstruction with entropy regularization to encourage opaque rendering [S1].
**Formula:**
The RGB loss is defined as:
$$ \mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {rgb}}=\left (1-\lambda _r\right ) \mathcal {L}_1+\lambda _r \mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {ssim}} $$
where $\mathcal{L}_1$ is L1 loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssim}}$ is SSIM loss, and $\lambda_r$ is the weight [S1].
The entropy loss on the foreground accumulated alpha value $\mathbf{O}_{\text{fg}}$ is:
$$ \mathcal {L}_{\text {entropy}}=-\sum \left (\mathbf {O}_{\text {fg}}\log \mathbf {O}_{\text {fg}}+\left (1-\mathbf {O}_{\text {fg}}\right ) \log \left (1-\mathbf {O}_{\text {fg}}\right )\right ) $$
The total loss is:
$$ \mathcal {L}=\left (1-\lambda _r\right ) \mathcal {L}_1+\lambda _r \mathcal {L}_{\mathrm {ssim}}+\lambda _e \mathcal {L}_{\text {entropy}} $$
**Parameters:**
$\lambda_r = 0.2$ and $\lambda_e = 0.1$ [S1].

## Background
Originating from early differentiable rendering works, photometric loss is the standard supervision signal for neural radiance fields. The inclusion of SSIM and perceptual losses (LPIPS) addresses the blurriness associated with pure L1/L2 losses [S1]. The integration of entropy regularization and visibility weighting was introduced to handle the ambiguity of background colors and occluded regions in volume rendering [S1]. Recent developments in dynamic radiance fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting have expanded this family to include flow regularization, total variation on density/depth, and scaling constraints to prevent degenerate primitives [S1, 9355-composite-photometric-and-regularization-loss].
